title: What are koans?
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching is that koans are not about achieving a special state or cutting off the mind, but rather about appreciating the present moment and letting go of habitual views. Koans can be seen as a way to smooth out our understanding of reality, much like concrete smoothing, by pointing us towards the ordinary nature of things. By embracing this perspective, we can gain new insights into the world around us and find freedom from preconceptions, rather than trying to grasp or understand them intellectually.

sentences.text: Good evening again.

Meo Zen did a wonderful introduction last week, but if you weren't here, you can probably tell from my accent: American Zen priest, also Soto priest, and the teacher of a similar sangha here in the States, in Washington State, in a town called Bellingham, north of Seattle, closer to Vancouver in Canada.
It's wonderful to be here again, so thank you to Meo Zen for inviting me to speak.
It's a bit of a leap of faith.
As far as I know he's never heard me say much of anything, so hopefully this won't cause too much confusion.
He won't have to give talks to repair the damage or something.

Lately I've been exploring the Zen koan literature a little more, and I'm just finishing a project to give a talk about all 48 of the koans in the most popular collection in Japan, called Mumon Kon in Japanese, Wumen Wan in Chinese.
It's a 13th century collection, put together by a Chinese teacher, and the name is actually kind of a play on his name.
Mumon Kon literally means "no door gate."
His name means "no door."
So it's like a gate or a barrier with no door in it.
Like life, you know?
I'm fond of this particular collection because this character, Mumon, is in my name, and Nomon is the same character.
For me it's "responding gate," which is a little easier to think about than "non-existing gate," but maybe also the same thing.
I don't claim to be a great koan master, but I know you mostly study Dogen, and that Myozan's taken on a similar little teaching quest.
It's impressive to try to give a talk on every fascicle in Shobogenzo.
That's a lot of study.
You don't have a day job, I guess.
Anyway, thinking about this, the audience I had in mind was committed Soto students who maybe aren't so familiar with koans, a little bit intimidated by them, maybe?
If that's not you, I apologize if you're much more familiar.
Maybe this will be less bang on, but hopefully there's something useful in here.
The first thing I want to think about with koans is to free us up a little bit.

When Japanese Zen first entered the western scene in the 50s and 60s, koan stories were one of the things that I think had the most confusion around them, tangled up with the idea that the Zen masters are enlightened in a certain kind of perfect, all-knowing way.

The koans got the rap of being merciless puzzles that are going to cut off our minds and frustrate the heck out of us for maybe a long time, but then lead to a great breakthrough of dazzling insight, ushering you to the other shore.
And after that, you'll be really happy all the time.
You could probably write a best-selling spiritual self-help book and start doing workshops, quit your day job.
Or, equally bad, a kind of hell: maybe we think that koans are merciless puzzles designed to cut off the mind, to frustrate us, and then eventually we break through.
Except, not for me.
I can't do it.
I'm not good enough, my meditation isn't strong enough, I don't have the right understanding or the right insight, or something is wrong with me.
I suck.
I don't think either of those models is that useful.
They're powerful stories, they're deep stories in a certain way.
There's much we can learn from them, and they're like the family stories of Zen, of Chinese Chan becoming Japanese Zen, Vietnamese Tien, Korean Song.
They were invented in China, so they're not an original Buddhist practice, actually.
Which is wonderful too.
Buddhism is a living tradition and has changed and grown over the centuries, over the millennia, and we're two more part of that dance now.
Hopefully we're contributing more than just confusion as we try to invent Zen in Ireland or in America.
So koans are sort of all that and none of that, in a way.
And in a way, everything is all that, and everything is none of that too, right?
On my jog this morning, I saw a crew who were finishing up a sidewalk, a walkway along the road.
There were a pair of workers doing the final smoothing of the wet concrete.
They were both men.
One guy was holding a long pole attached to a broad smoother device, like a big flat rubber mop.
The other guy was on the other side of the newly poured sidewalk, holding that in and carefully placing it down.
And the guy with the pole would very slowly, quietly, smoothly pull this smoother across the concrete, making the final finish.
The very last step of the job, I assume.
I haven't done a lot with concrete, I've done a little.
Around them, the other members of the crew were chattering away, like you do when you're working.
But these two guys were quiet.
They were focused.
They were very, very present.
And they were creating this beautiful, smooth, solid place for all of us to walk.
So I thought, well, that's just the same as our practice.
It's the same as studying koans, to study concrete smoothing.
I think if we appreciate koans deeply, we also need to appreciate that they're pointing to the same thing that everything else is.
It's a kind of category mistake to think that Zen, or any particular anything, is somehow special, or other than, or unique, or out of this world.
Because everything is all that.
Everything is ordinary and everything is unbelievable.
And that is one of the great qualities of koans, because when you study them, they start out looking one way, or they start out looking a little baffling, maybe.
Maybe if you joined that crew with no training, you'd be a little baffled by how to handle the concrete, right?
And if you screw it up, it's kind of permanent, right?
They have to break it out.
So they're pointers.
They're pointers with a certain kind of engagement with a deeper life, and a certain kind of reinvention or fresh understanding of who and what we are, moment to moment.
When we study koans, and any practices really, it can help pry us out of our habitual mind and our habitual views.
The term koan actually means "public case," like in the legal system.
Indirectly, I think it referred to the special desk where the magistrate would stand to issue judgment, in his peaked cap in old China.
So in Zen, they're also seen as precedent, or deep reminders.
This is the way it really is.
This is the natural law.
So they're pointers to the natural law of existence.
But actually, the origin before that is less official, and this is good to know too.

We think koans derive from party games, literary poetry games, where one old friend would start off the beginning of one poem and the other would answer with another poem in some congruous way according to rules of the game, because these were educated literati in China who had memorized many, many of the classics of Chinese literature.
And there's probably wine involved.
So it could be our holy koans actually are drinking games, which is perfect for Zen, too, of all the Buddhist traditions.
Even those Zen people, we must admit if we've been around them, do take themselves too seriously to a fault at times.
Actually, the tradition as a whole has this lighthearted, self-undermining quality, doesn't it?
These funny dialogues, and mock violence, and this holy literature that may have derived from a poetic drinking game.
So we take it seriously, but we also, I think, hold it lightly.
And probably this was continued in a similar fashion orally in the monasteries.
Monks hanging around.
If you've been in monasteries, you know there's a fair amount of hanging around.
They're not always sitting zazen, actually.
So monks hanging around and telling stories: "Hey, you know the one about old Master Zhaozhou?"
"Oh, yeah, well, what would Master Nanquan have said, like in this story?"
Kind of like us sitting around telling jokes.
In America, we have a bit of a stereotype that you Irish tell a lot more jokes than we do.
So one day I'll have to find out if that's true.
Are these stories literally true?
Well, we don't really know for sure.
The figures named all seem to be historical figures, as best as I can tell.
But whether that master exactly said that to that student, I think, is lost in the midst of time and a little dubious.
Because these are stories that are told over and over again, like family stories of your aunts and uncles.
In my family, my brother and I will never agree about who dropped the rock off the ferry on that trip that cracked somebody else's windshield down below.
My mom thinks it was my brother, but she always blamed him for things.
I'm pretty sure it was me, right?
We'll never know.
But it's a family story that...

So that's 600 years.
Here in America, we're trying to struggle through to 100-odd years, and we're having a hard time keeping our country together.
So 600 years, just a little slice of this ancient Chinese story.
Who knows what they really were originally, but they were written down, and now we have this written literature with the dense qualities that Chinese literature has.
They can remind us of things.
We can enter into these old stories in a way that... it moves me in ways that no other story does, actually, somehow.
And just as a reference, one of the most accessible books about this particular collection is this one.
I'll send you the reference.
The Gateless Barrier, Robert Aitken.
Wonderful American grandfather of Zen.

Sometimes we'll get together, a little group, two, three, four, five, not too many people.
We'll read the case and read one of the commentaries, like this one I just showed you, out loud.

I really recommend that.

Case five in Mumonkan is a classic Zen conundrum.
This is the kind of story that was emphasized in the 50s and 60s.
Here's case five.

verbatim.text: Good evening again, and so, Meo Zen did a wonderful introduction last week, but if you weren't here, you can probably tell from my accent, American Zen priest, also Soto priest, and the teacher of a similar sangha here in the States, in Washington State, a town called Bellingham, north of Seattle, closer to Vancouver in Canada. And it's wonderful to be here again. So thank you to Meo Zen for inviting me to speak. A bit of a leap of faith, as far as I know he's never heard me say much of anything, so hopefully this won't cause too much confusion. He won't have to give talks to repair the damage or something. So, lately I've been exploring the Zen koan literature a little more, and I'm just finishing a project to give a talk about all 48 of the koans in the most popular collection in Japan, called Mumon Kon, in Japanese, Wumen Wan, in Chinese, 13th century collection, put together by a Chinese teacher, and the name is actually kind of a play. The name of the book is kind of a play on his name. Mumon Kon literally means no door gate. His name means no door. So it's kind of like a gate or a barrier, with no door in it, you know? Like life, you know? And I'm kind of fond of this particular collection because this character, Mumon, is in my name, and no Mumon is the same character.
